title: Managing the Day
lessons/day-trading-u3-l1/steps/0/body: A pro day trader knows three numbers before the market opens: **risk per trade** (say 0.5 to 1% of the account), the **daily loss limit** and the **max number of trades**. If you hit the loss limit or the trade limit, **you're done for the day**.
lessons/day-trading-u3-l1/steps/1/body: The **chart** sets your stop loss distance, not the size you'd like to trade. Then you pick a size so a full loss equals your **risk amount**: **lots = risk amount ÷ (stop loss in pips × pip value per 1 lot)**.
lessons/day-trading-u3-l1/steps/2/prompt: Your account is $10,000 and you risk 1%. The stop loss on your EUR/USD trade is 25 pips. What's the right size in lots?
lessons/day-trading-u3-l1/steps/2/explan: 100 ÷ (25 × 10) = 0.4 lots. If the stop loss gets hit, you lose 25 pips × $4 = exactly $100.
lessons/day-trading-u3-l1/steps/3/prompt: How many pips is the stop loss from the entry on this buy trade?
lessons/day-trading-u3-l1/steps/3/explan: 1.0850 − 1.0832 = 0.0018, which is 18 pips. The stop loss sits just below the pullback low, so it only gets hit if the structure breaks.
lessons/day-trading-u3-l1/steps/4/statem: After hitting your daily loss limit, it's fine to keep trading with smaller size.
lessons/day-trading-u3-l1/steps/4/explan: A daily limit means a full stop. Trading on with smaller size still puts the same tired, upset mind back in the market.
lessons/day-trading-u3-l1/steps/5/prompt: Your daily loss limit is 2% and you risk 0.5% of the account per trade. If trades close at full losses, after how many trades is your day over?
lessons/day-trading-u3-l1/steps/5/explan: 2 ÷ 0.5 = 4. After four full losses in a row, you've hit your daily limit and have to call it a day.
lessons/day-trading-u3-l1/steps/6/senten: Position size = risk amount ÷ (stop loss distance × ___)
lessons/day-trading-u3-l1/steps/6/explan: Stop loss distance times pip value gives the loss on one lot. Divide your risk amount by that to get the number of lots.
lessons/day-trading-u3-l1/steps/7/prompt: Put the steps for sizing a day trade in order.
lessons/day-trading-u3-l1/steps/7/items/: Set the risk amount for this trade
Find your stop loss on the chart
Calculate the size with the formula
Place the order with its stop loss
lessons/day-trading-u3-l1/steps/7/explan: Risk and stop loss are the formula's two inputs, and size is its output. And an order never goes in without a stop loss.
lessons/day-trading-u3-l2/title: Closing Out Before the Day Ends
lessons/day-trading-u3-l2/steps/0/title: Why close before the day ends?
lessons/day-trading-u3-l2/steps/0/body: A position held through **rollover** (around 17:00 New York time) gets charged **swap** and faces **overnight news and gap risk**. Spreads also tend to widen around rollover. A day trader removes all of that by **closing on time**.
lessons/day-trading-u3-l2/steps/0/tip: In crypto futures, instead of swap there's “funding”, which most exchanges charge every 8 hours.
lessons/day-trading-u3-l2/steps/1/prompt: You hold a 2-lot position with a swap of $6 per lot per night. If you hold it for 3 nights, how much swap do you pay?
lessons/day-trading-u3-l2/steps/1/explan: 2 × 6 × 3 = $36. A day trader who closes before rollover never pays this cost at all.
lessons/day-trading-u3-l2/steps/2/statem: Daily forex rollover is around 17:00 New York time, and spreads usually widen then.
lessons/day-trading-u3-l2/steps/2/explan: Liquidity is thin around rollover and many liquidity providers widen their quotes, so the spread gets bigger for a few minutes.
lessons/day-trading-u3-l2/steps/3/body: Many day traders have a **cut-off time** (like an hour before the New York close, or the end of the overlap) when they close everything. A **time stop** means closing a trade if it hasn't worked out after a set amount of time.
lessons/day-trading-u3-l2/steps/4/prompt: It's 16:30 New York time and your plan's cut-off is 16:45. Your buy is 15 pips in profit but hasn't reached take profit. What do you do?
lessons/day-trading-u3-l2/steps/4/option: Hold till it hits target tomorrow
lessons/day-trading-u3-l2/steps/4/explan: Price has been flat for several candles and the day is ending. By the day-trading rule, you take the 15 pips. Holding until tomorrow turns a day trade into an unplanned overnight trade.
lessons/day-trading-u3-l2/steps/5/prompt: By closing all positions before the day ends, which cost or risk does a day trader remove?
lessons/day-trading-u3-l2/steps/5/option: The risk of losing during the day
lessons/day-trading-u3-l2/steps/5/explan: You pay spread and commission on every trade no matter what, and intraday risk is handled by your stop loss. What goes away is the cost and risk of holding overnight.
lessons/day-trading-u3-l2/steps/6/senten: Closing a position after a set time, even if it hasn't hit take profit or stop loss, is called a ___.
lessons/day-trading-u3-l2/steps/6/explan: A time stop closes trades whose idea hasn't played out, freeing up your capital and your focus.
lessons/day-trading-u3-l2/steps/7/prompt: Put a day trader's end-of-day routine in order.
lessons/day-trading-u3-l2/steps/7/items/: Open no new trades in the last half hour
Close positions and cancel pending orders
Log the day's results in your journal
Start tomorrow with no open positions
lessons/day-trading-u3-l2/steps/7/explan: First you stop new trades, then you close everything (a pending order could trigger overnight too), log it, and start the next day clean.
lessons/day-trading-u3-l3/steps/0/body: When the day is over, log every trade: a **screenshot** of entry and exit, the **setup**, the result in **R** (profit or loss divided by your initial risk) and whether it was **by the plan**.
lessons/day-trading-u3-l3/steps/1/prompt: Today's trades: +2R, −1R, −1R and +1.5R. What's the day's total?
lessons/day-trading-u3-l3/steps/1/explan: 2 − 1 − 1 + 1.5 = +1.5R. With $50 risked per trade, that's $75 profit.
lessons/day-trading-u3-l3/steps/2/body: A **good** trade follows the plan, even if it loses. A **bad** trade breaks the plan, even if it wins. Profit from a bad trade **reinforces** a bad habit, and sooner or later that gets expensive.
lessons/day-trading-u3-l3/steps/3/statem: A trade that followed the plan but lost counts as a bad trade.
lessons/day-trading-u3-l3/steps/3/explan: No setup wins every time. If you entered and exited by the plan, you did your job right. Losses are part of the cost of running a strategy with a positive edge.
lessons/day-trading-u3-l3/steps/4/prompt: Reviewing today's ORB: the first two candles made the range, and you bought on the third candle (which only wicked above the range) and lost. Tap the candle you should have entered on by the rules.
lessons/day-trading-u3-l3/steps/4/explan: The ORB rule is a body close outside the range. The third candle only had a wick and closed inside the range. This is the first candle that closed above 1.0866. Today's lesson: wait for the candle to close.
lessons/day-trading-u3-l3/steps/5/prompt: Two trades today: A followed the plan and made −1R. B had no setup, broke the plan and made +2R. Which behavior should you repeat?
lessons/day-trading-u3-l3/steps/5/option: A, because it followed the plan
lessons/day-trading-u3-l3/steps/5/explan: A single trade's result is mostly luck, but running a plan with a positive edge over hundreds of trades builds profit. B's win is a trap that reinforces the habit of entering without a setup.
lessons/day-trading-u3-l3/steps/6/prompt: Put the end-of-day review in order.
lessons/day-trading-u3-l3/steps/6/items/: Log all of today's trades with screenshots
Work out each trade's result in R
Mark which ones followed the plan
Write down one lesson for tomorrow
lessons/day-trading-u3-l3/steps/6/explan: Complete data first, then measurement, then judging your execution, and finally one practical takeaway to use tomorrow.
lessons/day-trading-u3-l3/steps/7/pairs/: A log of your trade details
An image of the chart at entry and exit
lessons/day-trading-u3-l3/steps/8/senten: If your initial risk is $40 and the trade makes $120, the result is ___.
lessons/day-trading-u3-l3/steps/8/explan: 120 ÷ 40 = 3, so you made three times your initial risk. Measuring in R makes trades with different sizes comparable.
